analysis.one_liner: Strengthens enforcement of equal pay for women by expanding damages, class actions, and wage transparency protections.
analysis.headline: Senate Republicans twice blocked the bill from reaching an up-or-down vote — 53-44 in April and 52-40 in September 2014 — and it died when Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have strengthened the Equal Pay Act, the 1963 law barring paying women less than men for equal work. It narrowed the excuses employers could use to justify a pay gap, added compensatory and punitive damages for workers who win discrimination suits, allowed pay-discrimination cases to proceed as class actions, and protected workers from retaliation for asking or talking about wages. It also directed the government to collect pay data by sex and race and to train women in salary negotiation. The bill never got a real vote: Senate Republicans twice voted down the procedural step needed to bring it to the floor, and it died when the 113th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Women workers who are paid less than male colleagues for equal work would gain stronger tools: the ability to sue for compensatory and punitive damages, to join class actions without signing individual consents, and to discuss wages without risking retaliation. The bill also funds negotiation-skills training for girls and women and requires federal collection of pay data by sex, race, and national origin.

how_it_helps.text: Narrows the employer's defense for a pay gap to 'bona fide factors' like education, training, or experience that are job-related and consistent with business necessity, and blocks the defense where a cheaper alternative practice exists.
Adds compensatory damages — and punitive damages where the employer acted with malice or reckless indifference — to the back-pay remedies workers can currently recover.
Allows pay-discrimination cases to be maintained as class actions under the federal rules, so workers can join without written consent.
Prohibits retaliation against employees who inquire about, discuss, or disclose their own or coworkers' wages.
Requires the EEOC to issue regulations collecting pay data by employees' sex, race, and national origin, and reinstates federal contractor pay-equity reporting.

analysis.who_pays: Employers covered by the Fair Labor Standards Act would bear higher litigation exposure — including class actions and punitive damages — plus new compliance costs from EEOC pay-data reporting and revised federal-contractor surveys. Small businesses exempt from the Fair Labor Standards Act are exempt here as well.

drawbacks.text: The bill exposes employers to uncapped punitive damages and broad class actions in pay-discrimination cases, a cost an honest supporter must acknowledge, particularly for companies with legitimate but hard-to-document pay structures.

It narrows the legal excuses an employer can offer for a pay gap and lets courts second-guess business decisions if an employee shows an alternative practice would work, which business groups argued would push pay decisions toward litigation defense rather than merit.
The EEOC pay-data reporting requirement imposes new recordkeeping and reporting burdens on employers, though the bill directs the agency to weigh those burdens when writing the rules.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers, the bill offered real, enforceable remedies for a problem the existing Equal Pay Act has struggled to reach — its damages are limited and its loopholes broad. The main cost falls on employers, especially larger ones, in litigation exposure and reporting; the bill gives small businesses exemptions and technical assistance to soften that. The trade-off is a genuine one, but the bill never got a fair test of it: it was stopped at the procedural stage both times.

outcome.mechanism: Senate Republicans twice blocked the bill from getting the 60 votes needed to cut off debate and bring it to the floor, so it never received an up-or-down vote and died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Mikulski introduced the bill on April 1, 2014, with 42 cosponsors (41 Democrats and 1 Independent).
On April 9, 2014, a procedural vote (cloture) to open debate failed 53-44, short of the 60 needed; no Republicans voted yes, and one Democrat joined most Republicans in opposition.
In September 2014 Democratic leaders revived the bill; the motion to proceed passed 73-25, with 19 Republicans joining.
On September 15, 2014, cloture on the bill itself failed 52-40, again short of 60, with all 39 voting Republicans opposed.
The bill never came to a vote on its merits and expired when the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who would have faced expanded damages, class actions, and pay-data reporting kept the existing, weaker Equal Pay Act rules. The majority of senators who supported the bill — 52-73 on various votes — never got the chance to vote it up or down.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers who opposed stronger equal-pay rules

for.name: Barbara Mikulski
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Paycheck Fairness Act and led the push for it in the Senate.

for.name: Harry Reid
for.what_they_did: Made motions to proceed to the bill in April, revived it on the floor in September, and forced two cloture votes on it.

for.name: 52 of 53 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Voted yes on the April 9 cloture vote to open debate on the bill.

for.name: 42 Senate cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors (41 Democrats, 1 Independent).

for.name: President Barack Obama
for.what_they_did: Publicly urged the Senate to pass the Paycheck Fairness Act during the 2014 debate.

against.name: 42 of 45 Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: Voted no on cutting off debate in April (53-44) and again in September (52-40), denying the bill the 60 votes needed to reach an up-or-down vote.

against.name: Mitch McConnell
against.what_they_did: Led the Republican opposition and voted no on both cloture votes that would have allowed the bill to proceed.

sides.party_line_note: Democrats voted nearly unanimously to advance the bill (52 of 53 in April, 51 of 53 in September), while every Republican who voted did so against it on both cloture votes, with 19 Republicans briefly joining on the September motion to proceed.

industries.note: The bill would have exposed covered employers to compensatory and punitive damages, broad class actions, a narrowed 'business necessity' defense, and new EEOC pay-data reporting. Those costs are the flip side of the remedies workers would gain, so the industry's interest ran against the bill's purpose.

The bill would have reinstated the Equal Opportunity Survey for nonconstruction contractors and required the contract-compliance office to use a broader set of investigative methods in pay-discrimination cases.

industries.industry: Small businesses exempt from the FLSA
industries.note: Small businesses already exempt from the Fair Labor Standards Act would have been exempt from this bill, and it directed agencies to develop compliance assistance materials for small business.
